pending_items.title: The photographs from Gaza that Sarajevo took home
pending_items.content:
Sarajevo, Bosnia and Herzegovina – A mother holds her daughter, trying to shield and comfort her at the same time. It is the eyes you notice first. And something aches deep inside you, especially if you come from Sarajevo, a city that survived a siege by Serb forces from 1992 to 1995.

Then you remember that you are still in Sarajevo, where there is peace now.

The image is the work of Salah Ostaz, who is still in Gaza, where rockets are falling and food and water are scarce, and where the silence of most world leaders may ring louder than the explosions, even as people in the streets around the world are raising their voices.

I have been a journalist for a long time. I took my first steps as a reporter in wartime Sarajevo: front lines, massacres, morgues, mass graves, hospitals, empty markets, cultural events that people risked their lives to attend for some semblance of normality. I wrote about all of it and thought nothing could get to me any more.

Another photograph. A girl’s eyes, wide open, as though she were looking back over the past three years at everything she has seen, which I do not even want to imagine.

In the next photograph, people line up for a spoonful of food.

And then something altogether different – children smiling and swimming at dusk off a crowded beach, as if this were the happiest time of their lives. There is hope in that picture.

That is what the people who organised Ostaz’s exhibition in Sarajevo believe. I went over to ask them how it came about.

Valida Hadzimuratovic, a radio journalist and DJ known in Los Angeles as Valida Carroll, was in Sarajevo when Ostaz video-called her in October last year. Alongside other activists, she had been organising weekly TikTok livestreams in which Palestinian journalists spoke about what they had witnessed. That call was the beginning of a friendship. Over the following months, she shared his photographs and learned more about his life, including why he had not been able to collect his diploma.

“I remember thinking how frustrating it must be to finish your studies, put in all that work, and then not be able to get hold of something as basic as your own diploma,” Valida told me.

She and her friend Nasiha, a Bosnian who also lives in Los Angeles, began raising money to cover his tuition fees. In September, they decided to show Ostaz’s work in Sarajevo. He sent them more than 150 photographs. Milomir Kovacevic, who documented life in his own city during the siege of Sarajevo, helped curate the show to include about 60.

A silent auction was held alongside the exhibition, with about two dozen artisans and small businesses donating work and prizes. Volunteers and activists from the Ka Gazi (Towards Gaza) movement helped organise the event.

Every Tuesday evening, Ka Gazi volunteers gather in central Sarajevo at the Eternal Flame, an antifascist memorial commemorating those who died resisting fascism during the Second World War. They read aloud the names of Palestinian children who have been killed. If you pass by, you hear the name of one child, then another.

Last year, the names were also read at Sarajevo’s MESS International Theatre Festival. The year before, the festival opened with Metro Gaza, a production featuring the Palestinian Freedom Theatre from Jenin, in the occupied West Bank. That year’s motto was “Unstoppable Life”.

“No one who lived through the siege of Sarajevo should be indifferent to the suffering of others,” said MESS director Nihad Kresevljakovic, while visiting the photography exhibition.

At the end of the evening, people walked out of the Bosnian Cultural Centre carrying photographs and items they had won at the auction. All the proceeds went towards covering the costs of getting Ostaz his diploma.

“We can’t help everyone in Gaza. The needs are enormous and the destruction is immeasurable. But we can help one person,” Hadzimuratovic said.

pending_items.title: 'Political theatre': Campaigners hit out at EU hypocrisy at Cop31
pending_items.content:
On Sunday, fraught global climate talks in Turkey , the longest ever in the climate conference’s history, ground to a halt, with no deal . The EU, UK and allies rejected the draft text over its failure to mention fossil fuels.

At the closing plenary, Ireland’s Climate Minister Darragh O’Brien, on behalf of the EU, rejected the text, saying it “does not respond to the science, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required… that does not even mention fossil fuels”.

His words were met with applause. But they rang hollow for developing countries, many of whom also rejected the text over its weak language on climate finance.

After delivering his intervention, O’Brien and EU Climate Minister Wopke Hoekstra walked out of the plenary to hold a press huddle while developing nations were speaking about the need for climate finance.

While the EU, UK and allies cited the omission of fossil fuels from the text as their main reasons for rejecting it, climate justice campaigners reported that developed countries and EU officials had spent the duration of the talks blocking measures which would require them to make fresh finance commitments.

“The EU used fossil fuels as the main reason for their rejection of the text. But the other issue, or what I would call the most important issue, is climate finance,” Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative and the global convenor of the Fill the Fund campaign, told Middle East Eye.

“If you listened to what other countries said, like Panama, Ghana, the Marshall Islands, their reasons were no money for adaptation, no money for loss and damage.”

Under the 2015 Paris Agreement, developed countries are required to provide finance to help developing countries cut emissions and adapt to climate impacts.

According to the UN’s latest report , published earlier this month, developing countries will need about $300bn annually in adaptation funding by 2035.

At Cop26 in 2021, developed countries agreed to at least double adaptation finance by 2025, with 2019 levels, $19bn, as a benchmark.

Last year, they agreed to a call to “at least triple” adaptation finance by 2035. But the final text left ambiguities around the baseline year.

An earlier draft of this year’s text, released on 16 November, stipulated a target annual figure of at least $120bn, with a baseline of $40bn a year.

But the sums were quietly dropped from subsequent drafts. Climate justice campaigners laid the blame for this squarely at the doors of the EU and wealthier countries who they say "came with nothing" and thwarted progress on discussions around climate finance.

During this year’s “Contributor Dialogue” at the conference, which aimed to fill the starved fund, a handful of developed countries pledged just $30m, significantly down from last year’s sum of $120m.

“So we have a fund that no one wants to fill,” Singh said.

Even before the summit had started, Hoekstra set the tone for negotiations by proclaiming climate finance “dead in the water”.

“They entered negotiations with that bad faith and blocked every single track which is important for developing countries,” Singh told MEE.

According to Climate Action network, the EU and other developed countries refused to engage on a baseline for tripling adaptation finance.

“We agreed on the baseline, I was witness to that process in 2019,” Singh said.

“So they just want to create new processes and new loops so that we can just continue talking.”

Singh also pointed to what he described as the hypocrisy of the EU and wealthy countries’ stance on fossil fuel language in the draft text.

"Norway and Ireland, who were arguing for the inclusion of fossil fuel language in the text, are back home expanding fossil fuel production,” he said.

The EU’s own “roadmaps” for transitions away from fossil fuels have drawn criticism for restating existing policies that are not aligned with the 1.5 degree temperature goal.

Brandon Wu, director of policy and campaigns at Action Aid USA, slammed the EU’s transition plans as a “smokescreen”.

“They’re using the rhetoric around fossil fuels to make themselves look like champions," Wu told reporters.

For Singh, a Cop veteran who has attended the last 18 conferences, the EU’s actions are tantamount to little more than “political theatre”.

“Do your work. We need to move beyond these theatrics and take real action, rather than simply claiming leadership. Be a real leader. Provide the money. Take action at home, in line with your fair share of the global effort.” he said.

Campaigners told Middle East Eye that the talks’ meltdown was also due in part to the weak and untransparent facilitation by the joint presidents, Australia and Turkey.

“There was no stocktaking plenary where countries could share their opinion, where things could be dragged out in the open. When they said they would publish text, they didn’t do so,” Andreas Sieber, associate director of global policy at 350.org, told MEE.

'Norway and Ireland, who were arguing for the inclusion of fossil fuel language in the text, are back home expanding fossil fuel production'

- Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Treaty Initiative

MEE understands that many developing countries felt they were left in the dark and not consulted while the text was being drafted.

Cop presidents usually release printed versions of drafts for parties to review. But this year, only selected groups were shown excerpts, leaving a lot of developing countries feeling “extremely disrespected and extremely badly treated,” one observer said.

Hanen Keskes of Greenpeace Mena said that the process of the revisions of the second draft of the Cop text was very unclear.

“From what I've heard from parties, they had not been consulted,” Keskes told MEE. “It was very unclear what progress happened between the 19th and 22nd on other agenda items that were quite important.

“When the new text came out on Saturday night, it was essentially the same text from the 19th. So clearly no consultation had been done.”

The acrimony was summed up in a searing rebuke of the Cop presidency by Ghana’s Environment Minister Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, who was “rudely cut off” during her delivery by Murat Kurum, Cop31 president and Turkey's environment minister.

“This excellency, is an example of the levels of disrespect we have endured and continue to express our objection to. It absolutely does not respect multilateralism,” she said.

pending_items.title: How the Iran war is reshaping the US military presence in the Middle East
pending_items.content:
The United States military presence across the Middle East is sprawling.

There are as many as 50,000 US troops and about 19 major military installations in the region, as well as assets spread across countries such as Bahrain, Jordan and Saudi Arabia.

But experts warn that the US-Israel war on Iran has exposed vulnerabilities in protecting Washington’s military assets in the region, leading some to speculate that a downsizing may occur once the war is over.

Michael O’Hanlon, senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, a Washington-based think tank, is among those who expect the US to eventually scale back its military presence in the Middle East.

“I think we will go smaller, more dispersed, more hardened, and generally further away from Iran — but not in each and every case,” O’Hanlon said.

As the war enters its 10th month on Saturday, the damage inflicted on US installations in the Middle East could one day translate into a strategic shift — not just for the US but for other countries that have been shaped by its military presence as well.

One of the long-term obstacles to maintaining the US military presence will be the cost of repairs.

Repairing damaged infrastructure on US bases in the region could cost $9.4b, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies, a Washington, DC-based think tank.

Hundreds of structures on US bases have been damaged by Iranian attacks since February 28, when the war began.

One of those bases was in Bahrain, home to the US Naval Forces Central Command and its Fifth Naval Fleet. The US has established a naval command presence in the country as far back as 1948.

But according to a report from the Congressional Research Service, the base — called Naval Support Activity (NSA) Bahrain — “sustained serious damage” in the early days of the Iran war. It estimated the cost of repairing the base at more than $400m.

Other US military assets in the region have also been impacted by the war .

In September, a Department of Defense inspector general report found the US had lost dozens of aircraft during the war, among them attack helicopters and sophisticated fighter jets like the F-35A and the F-15E.

By October, the total cost of the Iran war reached more than $47bn, according to Pentagon figures.

Rebuilding the US bases is unlikely until the Iran war is over, according to Mark Cancian, a senior adviser with the Defense and Security Department at CSIS.

“If the war ends with some sort of ceasefire or we get to a place where it’s somewhat stable,” Cancian said, “then you will see some reduction in US forces and reduction of the surge forces certainly and some rebuilding of the bases.”

But Cancian expects that the US will not rebuild all the military sites struck by Iran.

He pointed to the Bahrain headquarters of the Fifth Naval Fleet and the Combined Air Operations Center at Al Udeid airbase in Qatar as examples.

Some military facilities, he explained, will likely be moved underground to protect against aerial attack. Others may be relocated further from the Gulf, to places such as Israel or Jordan.

Major bases like those in Bahrain or Qatar were a liability because “they are right within the range of Iranian missiles and drones”, according to Kelly Grieco, a defence policy expert and senior fellow at the Stimson Center, a global security think tank.

But simply moving bases further away will not protect them in the long term. Grieco pointed out that Iran keeps improving its ability to reach longer-distance targets with drones and missiles.

One alternative to rebuilding bases, she said, would be instead to cultivate access to a network of airstrips and temporary bases in the Middle East that could be used if another conflict erupts.

In the Iran war, for instance, the US has relied extensively on facilities like Israel’s Ben Gurion airport for refuelling combat aircraft.

“What mattered more was access to places and the ability to move around those places, more than having a permanent operating facility,” Grieco said.

Experts say downsizing the US military presence in the Middle East has been a goal across several administrations.

President Donald Trump, for instance, has completed troop withdrawals from Syria and Iraq since the start of his second term in 2025. His predecessor, Joe Biden, also oversaw the US military pullout from Afghanistan in 2021.

But practical realities — including the emergence of new conflicts involving the US — have put that aspiration of a large-scale drawdown out of reach.

“The Biden administration wanted to reduce the force posture. The Trump administration wanted to reduce the force posture,” Cancian said. “They haven’t been able to, and it’s not clear they will be able to.”

Allies and adversaries alike also help to determine the heft of the US military presence, he added.

“The world gets a vote, and even if the administration wants to reduce the force posture, it may not be possible, because of continuing tensions,” Cancian said.

New alliances, however, have emerged that might make certain regional allies less reliant on US military resources.

In August, Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, a pact that theoretically commits the countries to come to each other’s aid in case of an attack.

Experts say the deal could trigger a regional realignment away from the US and its military might.

Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan could potentially wield formidable force : Together, they have more than 1.4 million active military personnel, own thousands of tanks and military aircraft and spend more than $124bn on their combined defence budget.

The pact is also likely to expand to include Egypt and Syria, further increasing its resources.

Such agreements might prove to be the first step in diversifying each country’s military strategy beyond their cooperation with the US, according to Grieco.

“The region had already been engaged in strategic diversification before this war started,” she said. “The real question moving forward is: Will they decide to pursue greater strategic dependence, or slowly decrease their dependence on the US for security?”

In the US, voter frustration could also disincentivise any effort to rebuild military installations in the Middle East.

The Iran war and US support for Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza have proven to be unpopular among the American public.

This month, for instance, the research firm Ipsos and the Reuters news agency found that 71 percent of Americans wanted Congress to end the war on Iran.

The conflict proved especially unpopular at the polls, with Trump’s Republican Party losing key races in the 2026 midterms to Democrats who were vocal in their opposition.

There was even backlash from within Republican ranks. Vice President JD Vance, who once touted his opposition to foreign wars, blamed the Iran conflict for his party’s poor showing in the midterm elections.

“The reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so,” Vance wrote on social media. “Everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there.”

Both parties are leaning away from a foreign interventionist stance, according to Grieco.

Although politicians are split over topics like US support for Israel, Grieco has observed that there is an overall inclination to extricate the US military from the Middle East.

“For most Americans, they’ve looked at the region since 1990 or 1991 and seen we are constantly conducting these interventions,” Grieco said. “None of them have gone well.”

pending_items.title: Between hope and grief, Palestinian families wait for sons' bodies
pending_items.content:
Palestinian construction worker Wael Sheghnoubi has been waiting in vain for his son Nidal's body since he was killed by the Israeli military in May 2025, unable to move on.

"When someone buries a martyr it brings relief. They haven't given us anything," said Sheghnoubi, holding a photo of his 16-year-old son in his home in the West Bank village of Burqa.

Israel's military frequently retains bodies of Palestinians, whether they are armed militants in Gaza or teens throwing rocks in the occupied West Bank.

The practice, which appears to have increased in recent years, leaves families torn between hope their relatives may be alive after all, and accepting their death.

"The army took the body away, and they didn't let anyone go near him. Of course, we remain worried, and we keep hoping," the father said, citing a case in which the military had misidentified a body and the man they had pronounced dead turned up alive in jail.

Nidal Sheghnoubi was shot by Israeli soldiers after the army said he and other teenagers threw stones at passing military vehicles.

His father sees the withholding of the body as a form of "punishment" directed at the broader community, but hopes for the best for his son.

"God willing, he'll turn out to be alive," he said.

According to the Jerusalem Legal Aid and Human Rights Center (JLAC), a Palestinian rights group, 807 Palestinian bodies are currently being held by Israeli authorities, including 678 from the West Bank and 105 from Gaza.

Hussein Shujaiya, coordinator of the Campaign to Retrieve the Bodies of Martyrs launched by JLAC in 2008, told AFP that hundreds more bodies of Palestinians killed during the Gaza war that began in 2023 have yet to be properly documented.

Shujaiya said the bodies are held in military morgues and cemeteries Palestinians refer to as "graves of numbers" because they include no names.

For Israel, the policy is designed to provide future leverage.

Its security cabinet decided in 2017 that certain Palestinian bodies could be held to be used as bargaining chips to aid the release of Israeli hostages, as was the case for some taken during Hamas's October 7, 2023 attack.

The decision was originally intended to apply to Hamas members or Palestinians who committed exceptional attacks, but the policy has come to be applied to civilians as well.

The military did not respond to AFP request for comment on the matter.

Back in Burqa, Iyad Daghlass sits surrounded by portraits of his 14-year-old son Motaz who was killed by Israeli forces the week before.

"They abducted the body. It's an extremely difficult feeling," Daghlass, a 52-year-old who also works in construction, told AFP.

Motaz went missing after an altercation with the military, which said he and other young people had been throwing stones at Israeli vehicles on the road near their village.

When a soldier told Iyad Daghlass that a boy had been found unconscious with two gunshot wounds, he hoped it would not be his son, but deep down felt it was his child.

"When she said that, I understood. Of course, I still wasn't entirely certain that it was my son."

The length of time that bodies are kept in military morgues has in recent times increased, leaving families in limbo.

Daghlass' brother Motaz, after whom he had named his son, was also killed by Israeli forces "in similar circumstances", in 2001.

"They withheld his body for three days before handing it over. But the situation wasn't as bad as it is nowadays," he said.

"Nowadays they hold bodies for one year, two years," he said, mentioning the case of another teenager from the village, killed in July 2025, whose body has yet to be returned.

In the village of Salem, one family finally found closure in November, when their son's body was returned after a year and a half.

Young villagers carried the body of Wissam Ishtayeh, who was 36 when he died in July 2025, after it was released at a hospital in the nearby city of Nablus.

His face had taken on a pale yellow tinge after more than a year in a morgue.

"Throughout all this time, we held on to the belief that he was in a hospital," Ghassan Ishtayeh told AFP shortly after his son was buried, wrapped in a Palestinian flag.

Wissam Ishtayeh was killed during an Israeli army raid that sparked clashes with residents, and was arrested while injured before Israeli authorities announced his death.

Despite the grief, Ghassan Ishtayeh said receiving his son's body had brought a form of relief to the family.

"All this time, we have been living with our nerves on edge, hoping that the day would come when we could know for certain, confirm the news one way or another, and finally find some peace."

pending_items.title: Explainer-What are the disputes between Iraq's federal government and Kurdistan region?
pending_items.content:
Nov 24 (Reuters) - Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi on Tuesday ordered federal authorities to take over border crossings in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region and directed the oil ministry to manage oilfields under Kurdish security control in four provinces, following an oil smuggling investigation at the state-run North Oil Company.

The orders are part of a broader crackdown byZaidi against oil smuggling. They also reopen long-running disputes between Baghdad and the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG) overcontrol of oil, money, territory and trade.

Though Baghdad says state oil marketer SOMO has sole authority to export Iraq's crude, for years the KRG exported independently through a pipeline to Turkey's Ceyhan port.

In 2014, Iraq took Turkey to arbitration at the Paris-based International Chamber of Commerce, which in 2023 ordered Ankara to pay Iraq about $1.5 billion for unauthorised exports between 2014 and 2018. Turkey shut the pipeline, halting about 450,000 barrels per day for two and a half years.

Flows resumed in September 2025 under an interim deal between Baghdad, theKRG and most foreign producers operating in the region. Under the deal, theKRG delivers crude to SOMO.

In August, Turkey and Iraq signed a one-year agreement maintaining use of the pipeline after the previous bilateral agreement expired. The arrangement covers capacity of 750,000 bpd while the two governments negotiate a longer-term deal.

Iraqi crude to Ceyhan averaged roughly 370,000 bpd in October, according to Turkish data.

The KRG began signing production-sharing contracts with foreign oil firms after the 2003 US-led invasion. However, in 2022, Iraq's Federal Supreme Court ruled the KRG's oil and gas law unconstitutional, ordered it to hand over oil production to Baghdad and authorised the federal oil ministry to pursue the invalidation of contracts signed under the regional framework. The KRG rejected the decision, and the contracts have remained the subject of litigation in Iraqi courts.

The 2025 interim export agreement sidestepped the underlying dispute over contracts by providing producers an interim $16 per barrel to cover production and transportation costs, pending an independent review of production costs.

Norway's DNO, the Kurdish region's largest producer, did not join the agreement and continued selling its production to local buyers at a discount to international prices.

Iraq relies on crude sales for more than 90% of state income. The KRG depends on federal budget transfers to pay public-sector salaries.

Baghdad, however, has delayed or withheld those transfers, accusing the Kurdish authorities of failing to hand over agreed oil and revenue. The KRG says Baghdad has not paid its full share.

During the pipeline shutdown and associated budget dispute, Kurdish public-sector workers faced repeated salary delays, while the regional government came under growing pressure to fund public services.

Tuesday's order directed the oil ministry to manage fields it said were under Kurdish regional security control in Diyala, Kirkuk, Salahuddin and Nineveh provinces.

Oil-rich Kirkuk lies outside the Kurdistan region's formal boundaries but is claimed by both sides. Kurdish forces took control of the province in 2014, and federal forces retook it in 2017 after the KRG held an independence referendum.

The Kurdish pipeline network gives the KRG leverage over northern exports. After the US-Israeli war on Iran severely restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, Iraq's oil output and exports fell sharply.

Baghdad asked to move federal crude from Kirkuk through the KRG-controlled pipeline network to Turkey. A senior KRG official said "no drop of oil" would pass unless Baghdad provided dollar relief for imports and security guarantees for oil companies.

Baghdad and the KRG reached an agreement in March to move Kirkuk crude through the Kurdish network to Ceyhan. And Iraq separately restored an older federal pipeline route from Kirkuk to Ceyhan. Exports through the route had been halted in 2014 after repeated attacks by Islamic State militants.

Iraq's oil minister said on November 17 that pumping through the rehabilitated route had begun at 120,000 bpd, with plans to raise flows gradually to 500,000 bpd.

Border crossings are a significant source of non-oil revenue for the KRG. Baghdad introduced an electronic customs system this year that lets it monitor imports and revenue in the region, a move the KRG saw as undermining its autonomy. It accused Baghdad of a "suffocating embargo" by restricting traders' access to dollars.

Zaidi's order to hand all crossings in the region to the federal border ports authority goes further.

In August, the KRG accused Dana Gas and Crescent Petroleum of breaching their contractual obligations by starting gas supplies from the Khor Mor field to Iraq's electricity ministry without its approval. The two companies had begun supplying 100 million standard cubic feet per day to the Kirkuk power station for a year.

The KRG said the decision was taken unilaterally and outside the contractual framework governing the project.

The companies denied any breach and said the KRG had been informed of the agreement in January.

(Reporting by Reuters; Editing by Joe Bavier)
